{"id": "5:90/q04", "question": "What is maysir?", "turns_on": "The notes differ between a general class of gambling, a broader distraction criterion, and specific pre-Islamic forms.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q04/p1", "position": "Gambling of every kind, including wagering with arrows, dice, chess and small games.", "reasons": "Mujahid includes Persian dice, arrows and every gambling kind; Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and others gloss gambling. Reports extend it to children's walnuts and eggs, knucklebones, chess and backgammon. Zajjaj, Wahidi and Study Quran identify camel gambling as its original or paradigmatic case. Ibn Qutayba explains yassartu and yāsir; Jishumi and Tabrisi derive it from yusr, ease, while Azharī says it first named the apportioned camel. Tabrisi also reports a folk etymology of the left hand as easing work by assisting the right."}, {"id": "5:90/q04/p2", "position": "Anything that distracts from God's remembrance and prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Qasim b. Muhammad gives this broader functional definition; it is reported by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Kathir."}, {"id": "5:90/q04/p3", "position": "The older usage includes arrow lotteries over wealth and produce, or trading meat for one or two sheep.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aʿraj gives arrow stakes; Saʿid b. al-Musayyib gives the meat exchange; Ibn Kathir repeats both."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q05", "question": "How did the old camel maysir work, and how many shares were there?", "turns_on": "The descriptions agree on arrow allotment but transmit twenty-eight, ten, or no known number.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q05/p1", "position": "A camel was slaughtered and divided by named arrows; winners received shares and could distribute them to the needy.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba locates it in harsh winter, ties the charitable benefit to 2:219, and says winners were praised while abstainers were called baram; Zajjaj describes wooden named arrows. Ibn ʿAtiyya notes the game offered pleasure and benefit; Abu Hayyan says defenders prized gains and victory; Qurtubi identifies commercial gain as a benefit."}, {"id": "5:90/q05/p2", "position": "The camel was divided into twenty-eight shares.", "reasons": "Al-Aṣmaʿī gives this number; Wahidi transmits the same dispute."}, {"id": "5:90/q05/p3", "position": "The camel was divided into ten shares.", "reasons": "Abu ʿAmr al-Shaybani gives this number; Wahidi transmits it."}, {"id": "5:90/q05/p4", "position": "The number of shares is unknown.", "reasons": "Abu ʿUbayda says he does not know; Wahidi transmits it."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q06", "question": "What are the anṣāb?", "turns_on": "Whether the erected objects are worshipped idols, sacrificial altars, or, in one report, games.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q06/p1", "position": "Erected idols or stones worshipped as idols.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, the majority in Mawardi and many later commentators identify worshipped idols; the root means upright, with naṣb singular and varying vocalization. Tabrisi cites al-Aʿsha's line about an erected idol. Alusi distinguishes unshaped worshipped stones from fashioned aṣnām; Asad extends the reference metaphorically to saint worship, magical objects and taboo."}, {"id": "5:90/q06/p2", "position": "Stones or altars at which animals were sacrificed to idols.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Abu Muslim specify sacrificial stones; Ibn ʿAbbas is so transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Kathir. Ibn ʿAtiyya says some accorded the stones special merit; the wife of al-Tufayl mentions Dhu al-Shara. Kuran Yolu locates stones around the Kaʿba; Study Quran ties the altars to 5:3."}, {"id": "5:90/q06/p3", "position": "Backgammon and chess.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports this as an alternative attributed to some, alongside idols."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q07", "question": "What are the azlām?", "turns_on": "The word is used for both divining and gambling lots; the 5:3 food context is al-Tabatabaʾi's deciding clue, while al-Azhari rejects the gambling identification here.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q07/p1", "position": "Divining arrows or lots consulted before undertaking an action.", "reasons": "Accounts give two marked commands, three arrows marked yes, no and blank, and arrows kept at the Kaʿba; Suraqa used them during the Hijra. Bukhari says a zalam lacks feathers. Divination concerned travel, war, residence and trade. Kuran Yolu calls it predictive and opposed to monotheism."}, {"id": "5:90/q07/p2", "position": "Pebbles used as lots for whether to go on a campaign or stay.", "reasons": "Saʿid b. Jubayr reports pebbles; al-Thawri is reported similarly."}, {"id": "5:90/q07/p3", "position": "Arrows or other implements used to allot gambling shares.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports this but says al-Azhari rejects the identification; Ibn ʿAtiyya and Tabrisi acknowledge gambling arrows, while Elmalılı includes sticks and dice. Al-Tabatabaʾi prefers lottery arrows because of 5:3's food context and says the word would otherwise be ambiguous; he opposes taking the verse as a ban on istikhara."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q08", "question": "What does rijs mean here?", "turns_on": "The glosses emphasize repulsiveness, sin or evil, divine displeasure, or the resulting legal ban.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q08/p1", "position": "Filth or something vile and repugnant, chiefly moral or religious foulness in this context.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba gives stench as root sense; Zajjaj and Wahidi describe ugly deeds and a loud-sound root attested by a poet's rajjās and thunder clouds. Tabrisi, Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Samin and Alusi preserve that derivation. Ibn ʿAtiyya distinguishes rijz punishment and riks excrement, while Ibn Durayd calls rijs evil. Bursevi contrasts rational repugnance with natural najās. Ibn ʿAshur includes visible and inward filth and cites 9:125 and 33:33. Al-Tabatabaʾi says benefits in 2:219 do not yield lasting good."}, {"id": "5:90/q08/p2", "position": "Sin or evil.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls it sin; Ibn Zayd and Zayd b. Aslam evil; Saʿid b. Jubayr sin."}, {"id": "5:90/q08/p3", "position": "God's displeasure or wrath.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbas gives this gloss in Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn ʿAtiyya, Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir."}, {"id": "5:90/q08/p4", "position": "That which is forbidden.", "reasons": "Mawardi derives the legal sense from basic filth and prohibition."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q09", "question": "What does the singular predicate rijs describe, and why is it singular?", "turns_on": "The issue is whether a singular generic predicate directly covers all four nouns or ellipsis supplies a genitive or repeated predicates.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q09/p1", "position": "It predicates filth of all four named things directly; as a generic noun or verbal noun it can remain singular.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin say direct predication is stronger and compare 9:28; Alusi says the verbal noun does not vary in number, and Ibn ʿAshur says the singular identifies the items with filth."}, {"id": "5:90/q09/p2", "position": "An omitted genitive such as the affair, use, or action of the four things is the subject described as filth.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa supply the omitted term; Tabrisi spells out drinking or handling wine, worshipping idols and drawing lots. Abu Hayyan and Samin reject the need for deletion."}, {"id": "5:90/q09/p3", "position": "Rijs predicates wine alone, with predicates of the remaining coordinated nouns understood by ellipsis.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa, Baydawi, Biqaʿi and Alusi give this parse; Biqaʿi says one collective predicate is insufficient."}, {"id": "5:90/q09/p4", "position": "Rijs predicates the last noun, with earlier predicates elided.", "reasons": "Samin gives the reverse parse and compares 9:62."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q10", "question": "How does min ʿamal al-shayṭān attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "The grammatical force of min and whether an omitted genitive changes the causal reading.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q10/p1", "position": "It qualifies rijs as an adjective in the nominative sense.", "reasons": "Samin gives the iʿrāb; Alusi adds that min can mark causal origin in Satan's temptation."}, {"id": "5:90/q10/p2", "position": "Min marks origin from Satan's work.", "reasons": "Alusi allows this alternative and questions the claim that an omitted genitive makes causal connection or originative min unnecessary."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q11", "question": "In what sense are these things Satan's work?", "turns_on": "Whether attribution means his incitement or his origination of the practices.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q11/p1", "position": "Satan invites, adorns, and incites people to the practices, although the physical things are God's creation.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Abu Hayyan compare 28:15; Tabari says God neither urges nor approves them. Tabrisi links intoxication with loss of reason, gambling with base traits, idols with shirk and lots with poor judgment. Razi cites 9:28 and 24:26 for impurity's association. Ibn ʿAshur and others call the attribution an intensification of repulsion."}, {"id": "5:90/q11/p2", "position": "Satan originated the practices and people followed him.", "reasons": "Qurtubi offers this alongside incitement and embellishment."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q12", "question": "What does ijtanibūhu mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q12/p1", "position": "Keep apart from it, put it to one side, and leave the condemned practices.", "reasons": "Tabari says reject and refrain; Wahidi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Biqaʿi explain the spatial image of keeping apart; Bursevi applies it to impurity."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q13", "question": "To what does the singular pronoun in 'avoid it' refer?", "turns_on": "The singular can resume the unified predicate, the whole list, an implied act, or Satan's work; direct reference is defended as rhetorically stronger.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q13/p1", "position": "It refers to rijs, the unified filth covering all four items.", "reasons": "Saʿid b. Jubayr says the phrase em

braces the list; Wahidi, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAshur give rijs as antecedent; Abu Hayyan and Samin prefer direct reference as stronger, with the fāʾ consequence noted by Ibn ʿAshur."}, {"id": "5:90/q13/p2", "position": "It refers to the named things collectively.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Nasafi give this as a possibility; Ibn ʿAshur says the command concerns their harmful intended use."}, {"id": "5:90/q13/p3", "position": "It refers to an omitted noun meaning their conduct, consumption, or practice.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Abu al-Baqa and Razi offer the ellipsis; Abu Hayyan rejects its necessity, and Samin prefers direct reference."}, {"id": "5:90/q13/p4", "position": "It refers to Satan's work, or Satan himself.", "reasons": "Tabrisi and Nasafi allow Satan's work; Alusi also mentions Satan himself."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q14", "question": "What force does the command to avoid these practices have?", "turns_on": "The command's imperative force is accepted; the disputed auxiliary inference is whether the word rijs alone yields prohibition.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q14/p1", "position": "It establishes a binding prohibition of wine, gambling, idol rites and divining lots.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Saʿid b. Jubayr compare avoiding idols in 22:30; Ibn ʿAtiyya and Qurtubi add hadith and consensus. Tabrisi gives four proofs: impurity, Satanic attribution, imperative abstention and success conditioned on avoidance. Qurtubi says command and rebuke are stronger than the declarative ban of 6:145; Ibn ʿAshur reads the listed harmful uses as prohibited."}, {"id": "5:90/q14/p2", "position": "The label rijs itself proves prohibition by analogy to other forbidden filth.", "reasons": "Some invoke 6:145's carrion, blood and pork; Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan report the inference as problematic."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q15", "question": "What does 'so that you may prosper' promise?", "turns_on": "The glosses identify success as prosperity and reward, with one report emphasizing meeting God.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q15/p1", "position": "Abstention is a means to success, reward and prosperity with God.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Saʿid give the simple gloss; Tabari explains prosperity with God and cross-refers 2:189. Muhammad b. Ishaq specifies escaping punishment and gaining promised reward; Tabrisi says winning reward; Biqaʿi says attaining aims. Ibn ʿAshur adds that other persistent sins condition hope and compares 2:21. Kashshaf and Nasafi infer indulgence entails ruin."}, {"id": "5:90/q15/p2", "position": "The phrase expresses hope of meeting God tomorrow.", "reasons": "Muhammad b. Kaʿb al-Qurazi gives this eschatological gloss."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q16", "question": "Why this emphatic wording and sequence of the four practices?", "turns_on": "Different explanations focus on cumulative emphasis, the leading position of wine, a progression of harms, or shared pagan custom.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q16/p1", "position": "The stacked expressions reinforce the ban, especially on wine and gambling, by placing them with pagan rites and tying avoidance to success.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and al-Tabatabaʾi enumerate innamā, idols, filth, Satan, the imperative and success; Zamakhshari adds 22:30. Ibn ʿAtiyya says idols in the list make other practices base. Wahidi, Tabrisi and multiple hadith comparisons liken drinkers to idol worshippers. Bursevi and Elmalılı say wine and gambling are the chief target; Zamakhshari says 5:91 singles them out. Ibn ʿAbbas reports Companions equated wine with shirk. Burhan reads the wording as a reordered call to abstain from idols as impurity."}, {"id": "5:90/q16/p2", "position": "Wine comes first because the occasion concerned its harms and it encompasses sin.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives this reason for the order."}, {"id": "5:90/q16/p3", "position": "The order follows linked corruptions: wine wastes wealth, gambling corrupts wealth, idols show open shirk and arrows hidden shirk.", "reasons": "Biqaʿi develops this pairwise order and says all are pagan customs sharing worldly and religious harm."}, {"id": "5:90/q16/p4", "position": "The four are grouped because all were pre-Islamic polytheist customs requiring avoidance.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari states this grouping; Abu Hayyan says altar stones remove lingering reverence or idol grouping assimilates the other practices. Kuran Yolu warns about shrine vows, graveside sacrifices and modern superstitions."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q17", "question": "What harms and benefits of wine and gambling explain the ban?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q17/p1", "position": "Their limited apparent benefits are outweighed by moral, social and religious harms.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan records claims of wine relieving worry, giving courage and generosity and gambling yielding wealth, then says wine destroys reason and wealth and leads to killing, hatred and sins while gambling takes wealth unjustly; a poet illustrates waste. Kashshaf and Razi point to 5:91's enmity and diversion from remembrance and prayer. Kuran Yolu adds observable social and bodily harm and argues moderate use cannot control the greater harm; al-Tabatabaʾi says 2:219's benefits have no lasting human good."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q18", "question": "Are small quantities of intoxicating non-grape drinks forbidden?", "turns_on": "The dispute concerns whether the non-grape drink's small amount follows its intoxicating large amount; the necessity note concerns exceptional need.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q18/p1", "position": "Yes: any drink intoxicating in a large amount is forbidden even in a small amount.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu Hayyan report the majority; both report consensus for any small or large amount of pure grape wine. Biqaʿi states no amount distinction; Ibn Kathir transmits every intoxicant unlawful; al-Tabatabaʾi transmits every intoxicant as wine."}, {"id": "5:90/q18/p2", "position": "A non-intoxicating amount of a non-grape drink may be consumed even if much would intoxicate.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa and some Kufans hold this; Ibn ʿAtiyya rejects it. Abu Hayyan notes the dispute."}, {"id": "5:90/q18/p3", "position": "Dire necessity can permit otherwise banned intoxicants.", "reasons": "Asad restricts the exception to unavoidable need such as illness or accident, citing 5:3."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q19", "question": "Do chess, backgammon and games without stakes fall under the ban?", "turns_on": "Whether the shared harms suffice to extend the prohibition to unstaked games; the juristic rulings differ.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q19/p1", "position": "Yes, even without stakes, because they invite obsession, hostility and distraction from prayer and remembrance.", "reasons": "Qurtubi extends wine and gambling's common rationale; Ibn Kathir transmits hadith against nard, grades one marked-dice report gharīb, notes Abu Musa's report may be his own statement, and lists Malik, Abu Hanifa and Ahmad as forbidding chess. Ibn ʿUmar says chess worse than nard. Al-Qasim's maysir definition is functional."}, {"id": "5:90/q19/p2", "position": "Chess is disliked rather than categorically forbidden.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports al-Shafiʿi's ruling; Study Quran says neither chess nor backgammon was legally banned and both remain popular."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q20", "question": "Is wine itself ritually impure?", "turns_on": "Whether rijs denotes physical impurity and what to infer from street disposal.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q20/p1", "position": "Yes: its description as rijs and the order to avoid it establish impurity.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports the majority and defends inference from general texts and analogy; he replies that Medina's road disposal was practical because homes lacked wells and latrines and also publicly showed destruction."}, {"id": "5:90/q20/p2", "position": "No: wine is pure as a substance, while drinking it is prohibited.", "reasons": "Qurtubi attributes this to Rabiʿa, al-Layth, al-Muzani and others; Saʿid b. al-Haddad cites Companions pouring it into Medina's streets with no prophetic ban on doing so. Qurtubi rejects that inference."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q21", "question": "Does avoidance prohibit wine ownership, sale and other uses?", "turns_on": "The disagreement turns on whether the command excludes every utility or only the objects' harmful intended use.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q21/p1", "position": "Yes: wine must be abandoned, sold neither directly nor for profit, and has no lawful ordinary utility.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites the Prophet's refusal of a wine gift and order to pour it out; he infers no ownership or sale, and reports consensus against selling wine and blood. Tabrisi includes buying, selling and all dealings; Ibn Kathir transmits multiple pour-out and market-container reports, a refusal to return or gift stock, and prohibitions on its price; Thaʿlabi transmits curses covering makers, traders, carriers and drinkers. Study Quran includes sale proceeds. Ibn Kathir calls the Khaybar carrier report gharīb and notes Bahrain compensation for orphans and reuse of emptied vessels. Qurtubi compares the permitted use of a tanned dead sheep hide and extends the wine-sale analogy to animal dung, recording Malik's dislike, Ibn al-Qasim's permission for utility, and the Shafiʿi agreement with Malik."}, {"id": "5:90/q21/p2", "position": "Wine can be owned for limited utility such as relieving choking or extinguishing fire.", "reasons": "Ibn Khuwayz Mindad attributes this to Malik; Qurtubi says the attribution is unknown and follows only if wine is held pure, then rejects it because the Prophet ordered pouring it away."}, {"id": "5:90/q21/p3", "position": "Avoidance concerns harmful intended uses, not mere touching, showing or historically preserving the objects.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur gives examples of inspection, display, historical preservation and allowing wine to become vinegar."}]}

 converted into vinegar or used as a preserve?", "turns_on": "The dispute concerns deliberate alteration after the order to pour wine away, with separate distinctions for spontaneous vinegar and other preserves.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q22/p1", "position": "Vinegar formed by itself is lawful, but a Muslim should pour wine out rather than deliberately convert it.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports Malik, ʿUmar, Qabisa, Ibn Shihab, Rabiʿa and Shafiʿi positions on spontaneous vinegar and endorses Malik's ban on treatment. Majority jurists prohibit treatment; reports from ʿUthman b. Abi al-ʿAs and Anas describe prophetic refusal even for orphans' wine. Qurtubi argues the order to empty it would make no sense if conversion were lawful."}, {"id": "5:90/q22/p2", "position": "Wine may be deliberately converted to vinegar, then eaten.", "reasons": "Thawri, Awzaʿi, al-Layth and Kufans allow conversion; a report from Ashhab says Malik permits Christian-made vinegar and the same from a Muslim who should repent. Qurtubi allows that an early ban might have targeted new drinking habits."}, {"id": "5:90/q22/p3", "position": "Wine may be made into a changed preserve with musk or salt.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa permits it if wine's state changes; Iraqis cite a weak report from Abu al-Darda about sun and salt tanning it."}, {"id": "5:90/q22/p4", "position": "Treatment is confined to making vinegar, not other preserves.", "reasons": "Muhammad b. al-Hasan states this narrower allowance; Qurtubi notes opposition by ʿUmar and ʿUthman b. Abi al-ʿAs to conversion."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q23", "question": "What practices analogous to arrows and idols are included or excluded?", "turns_on": "Whether a guidance practice claims divination or merely resolves practical hesitation while relying on God.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q23/p1", "position": "Augury, written omens and shrine customs resemble the condemned pagan reliance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan mention bird augury and omens from books; Kuran Yolu cautions against shrine vows and sacrifices at graves, and modern lottery superstition. Asad reads anṣāb as idolatry broadly."}, {"id": "5:90/q23/p2", "position": "Istikhara and favorable omens after thought and consultation are permissible guidance, not forbidden azlām.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabaʾi cites Sunni and Shiʿi reports on the Prophet welcoming good omens and Ahl al-Bayt reports allowing rosary guidance. He says the practice ends indecision, claims no hidden knowledge or divine governance, and is not a binding ruling; its outcome can still be good or bad."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q24", "question": "What incident prompted this verse?", "turns_on": "The transmitted occasions name different people and incidents; Kuran Yolu says no specific cause is certain.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q24/p1", "position": "Saʿd b. Abi Waqqas was struck with a camel jawbone after drinking and tribal boasting, then complained to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Muqatil names ʿUthban b. Malik; the reports vary whether Saʿd was struck on nose or head, and whether an Anṣari hosted. Wahidi says Muslim transmits Saʿd's account. Elmalılı adds that Saʿd recited satire. Al-Tabatabaʾi observes public accounts differ sharply."}, {"id": "5:90/q24/p2", "position": "Two Anṣari clans became drunk and fought, then blamed each other for injuries and acquired rancor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbas reports this through Mawardi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan, Suyuti and Durr; Durr adds the later 5:93 question. A broader report says Muslims drank, fought and spoke offensive words."}, {"id": "5:90/q24/p3", "position": "ʿUmar repeatedly prayed for a clear ruling, received successive wine passages, and declared 'we have stopped.'", "reasons": "Abu Maysara and ʿUmar reports describe 2:219, 4:43 and the final verse; Elmalılı repeats his response."}, {"id": "5:90/q24/p4", "position": "Hamza's intoxicated attack on ʿAli's camels occasioned the prohibition.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports the incident; a report from Jaʿfar al-Ṣadiq names sakarkah, places revelation before Uhud and includes Hamza's reconciliation and martyrdom. Its continuation recounts his shroud and conduct at Uhud."}, {"id": "5:90/q24/p5", "position": "An intoxicated Companion's misrecitation at Maghrib helped prompt the final ban.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives this occasion; Abu Hurayra and Suyuti place drunken misrecitation before 4:43 in a staged account."}, {"id": "5:90/q24/p6", "position": "ʿUmar drank, struck ʿAbd al-Raḥman b. ʿAwf and lamented Badr's dead before the final revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabaʾi reports Zamakhshari's staged narrative."}, {"id": "5:90/q24/p7", "position": "Hostility after gambling losses may have been an occasion.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu reports Tabari listing this with ʿUmar and Saʿd and saying no cause is certain."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q25", "question": "When and through what stages was wine prohibited?", "turns_on": "The notes disagree on the count and order of prior passages, whether prior rules were abrogated, and the date of this revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q25/p1", "position": "A staged sequence culminated here: 2:219, then 4:43, then this decisive prohibition.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Hurayra, Saʿid b. Jubayr, Qurtubi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, Ibn ʿAshur and others recount benefits acknowledged, prayer-time restraint and final abstention; 5:93 reassured about those who died before the ban. Qurtubi calls 2:219 and 4:43 abrogated; Elmalılı calls this third and final. Kuran Yolu invokes ʿAʾisha's warning against an abrupt initial ban and compares failed American prohibition. Qurtubi says apparent pre-ban permission conflicts with the juristic claim that every religious law forbade intoxication, which jurists ground in reason's role in welfare."}, {"id": "5:90/q25/p2", "position": "There are four wine-related revelations, with 16:67 also counted before the final passage.", "reasons": "Bursevi calls this fourth; Study Quran orders 16:67, 2:219, 4:43 and 5:90. Al-Shaʿbi instead gives 2:219 then 16:67 then al-Maʾida; al-Tabatabaʾi rejects the implied abrogations."}, {"id": "5:90/q25/p3", "position": "The law was always prohibited; the progression was in manner of address and practical obligations, without legal abrogation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabaʾi says 7:33 and 2:219 already prohibit, with 4:43 a particular warning, and rejects al-Shaʿbi's abrogation chain; Abu Jaʿfar says every prophet's mission included wine's ban, while people were moved gradually to avoid abandonment of religion."}, {"id": "5:90/q25/p4", "position": "The prohibition was revealed after Uhud in year three of the Hijra.", "reasons": "Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn ʿAshur give this dating; Ibn ʿAshur says the verse was then placed later in al-Maʾida."}, {"id": "5:90/q25/p5", "position": "The prohibition came a few days after the Battle of the Trench.", "reasons": "Biqaʿi reports al-Aṣbahani's date."}, {"id": "5:90/q25/p6", "position": "The ban is Medinan and among the last revelations of al-Maʾida.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports Muslim agreement; al-Tabatabaʾi calls these the latest wine-ban verses."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q26", "question": "When did a new prohibition bind someone who had not yet heard it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q26/p1", "position": "It binds when news of abrogation reaches the person.", "reasons": "Qurtubi explains a man gifting wine while unaware of the ban and the people of Quba changing prayer direction on receiving news; he endorses this timing."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q27", "question": "How did hearers react when the prohibition was announced?", "turns_on": "The reports distinguish communal response at the ban from one man's earlier abstention.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q27/p1", "position": "They immediately desisted and poured out wine.", "reasons": "Anas says jars of date wine were emptied without further question; Burayda reports companions draining remaining cups and pouring out stores; Abu Hurayra says the Prophet announced the ban after earlier hinting a ruling would come. ʿUmar said they had stopped."}, {"id": "5:90/q27/p2", "position": "ʿUthman b. Maẓʿun had renounced wine even before Islam and lamented its loss when the verse was recited.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Rahman b. Sabit says he feared intoxication would cloud reason and lead to unwanted marriage."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q28", "question": "What warnings and prophetic reports reinforce the wine prohibition?", "turns_on": "These are distinct reports and warnings, not competing legal interpretations; their details and stated chain assessments differ.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q28/p1", "position": "Wine brings severe moral and afterlife consequences for drinkers and those helping its trade.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabi transmits deprivation of Paradise wine, venom, rejected worship until repentance, curses for production and trade, no coexistence of wine and faith, idol-worship likeness, mistrust and reputational harm; a poet says nabidh opens evil. Ibn Abi Hatim reports Judgment Day thirst for drinkers and drink for abstainers. Ibn Kathir gives later reports on lost prayer, forty mornings, Hell's extract, deprivation of Paradise wine, God not looking at habitual drinkers, and Paradise barred; he notes Bukhari's chain doubts for one report. ʿUthman recounts an ascetic driven to adultery and murder by wine."}, {"id": "5:90/q28/p2", "position": "This verse has a Torah counterpart abolishing play, music, dancing, instruments, songs and wine.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allah b. ʿAmr transmits the claim; Ibn Kathir grades the chain sound."}, {"id": "5:90/q28/p3", "position": "Reports also prohibit associated drinks, instruments and gambling.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports bans on kubah, qinin or lutes, mizr and ghubayra, with two reports transmitted by Ahmad alone; a separate report names wine and gambling."}, {"id": "5:90/q28/p4", "position": "A questioner was told he was among those who do good.", "reasons": "Muqatil rep

orts the Prophet's reply without identifying the question in this excerpt."}, {"id": "5:90/q28/p5", "position": "Had earlier scriptures and prophets continued, the community would have received an especially severe wine ban.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbas says its matter is deferred to Judgment Day."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q29", "question": "How does the verse connect with nearby rulings and other passages?", "turns_on": "The links operate at different scales: preceding permission, earlier lexical discussions, and the following explanation and reassurance.", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q29/p1", "position": "After allowing lawful foods and warning against self-denial, the passage identifies truly forbidden drink and pagan practices.", "reasons": "Tabari recalls companions who renounced lawful women, sleep and meat at 5:87; Razi and Abu Hayyan link 5:87–88 with the ban; Tabrisi says it turns from pre-Islamic custom to Islamic law; Biqaʿi says drink follows food and compares 5:3. Elmalılı says avoid unlawful impurity after refusing to ban wholesome things. Study Quran notes these are the sura's wine and gambling rulings."}, {"id": "5:90/q29/p2", "position": "The verse recalls earlier explanations of wine, gambling, altars and arrows in al-Baqara and at 5:3.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, Razi, Qurtubi, Tabrisi, Baydawi, Biqaʿi, Bursevi and Elmalılı point back; the repeated cross-references carry lexical details rather than fresh disagreement."}, {"id": "5:90/q29/p3", "position": "The next verse specifies hostility, hatred and neglect of remembrance and prayer, while 5:93 answers concern for earlier drinkers.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi and al-Tabatabaʾi tie 5:91 to worldly and religious harms; Abu Hurayra's report supplies 5:93's reassurance. Al-Tabatabaʾi says the verses form a coherent, nearly simultaneous unit; Samarrai compares added warning and knowledge in al-Maʾida to al-Taghabun's lack of a prior comparable ban."}]}
{"id": "5:90/q30", "question": "What inward lessons are drawn near this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "5:90/q30/p1", "position": "A seeker should surrender to God's decree and serve steadily rather than demand closeness by oath.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites al-Taʾwilat al-Najmiyya: an oath from intense longing is excused yet idle under contentment and a lapse under surrender; the seeker should accept approach or estrangement. Persian verse, Ibn al-Farid and the Mathnawi urge prompt use of time and patience in hardship."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q01", "question": "Who is addressed by the command?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular address is confined to Muhammad, includes believers by shared cause, or addresses them through him.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q01/p1", "position": "The Prophet and all believers are included.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Kuranyolu cite the shared danger of hearing mockery. Ibn Kathir applies it to every community member; Islahi cites 6:69 and 4:140."}, {"id": "6:68/q01/p2", "position": "The Prophet is addressed formally, but believers are intended.", "reasons": "Biqaʿi says addressing him deters others. Some compare 39:65; Ibn al-ʿArabi rejects that analogy because prophetic forgetting is possible."}, {"id": "6:68/q01/p3", "position": "The Prophet alone is intended.", "reasons": "Ibn Jarir explains that his visible departure rebukes and troubles the polytheists; believers' departure would not."}, {"id": "6:68/q01/p4", "position": "Any listener is directly addressed.", "reasons": "Razi and Abu Hayyan transmit this alternative; Kuranyolu records Muslims other than the Prophet as addressees."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q02", "question": "What does 'see' mean and how is its clause construed?", "turns_on": "Whether seeing is physical perception or knowledge, and whether the active verb already supplies the circumstantial state.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q02/p1", "position": "It means physically seeing them engaged in mockery.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan treats it as a one-object verb with an omitted circumstantial state. Samin says yakhudun is already circumstantial, so another state is redundant; Ibn Ashur describes seeing active polemic."}, {"id": "6:68/q02/p2", "position": "It means hearing their talk.", "reasons": "Muqatil addresses this explanation to Muhammad."}, {"id": "6:68/q02/p3", "position": "It could mean mental knowledge, requiring an omitted second object.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls this remote, citing grammarians who forbid or rarely allow such omission; Samin records the Sheikh's objection and stricter grammatical opinions."}, {"id": "6:68/q02/p4", "position": "A separate omitted circumstantial state must be supplied.", "reasons": "The Sheikh reads seeing them while engaged; Samin rejects the extra ellipsis because yakhudun or the active-participle force of the relative clause suffices."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q03", "question": "How do the temporal clauses and responses work?", "turns_on": "Whether emphatic nun is obligatory with conditional imma, and whether idha itself makes the rule iterative.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q03/p1", "position": "Imma is conditional in plus added ma and normally takes emphatic nun, though omission occurs.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Samin cite a poetic line beginning imma yusibka ʿadu; Bursevi explains assimilation of in's nun; Tabatabaʾi calls ma emphatic or mitigating; Alusi cites Ibn Durayd."}, {"id": "6:68/q03/p2", "position": "The first time clause is governed by 'turn away'; imperative responses have general force.", "reasons": "Samin and Bursevi assign idha accusative force through fa-aʿrid; Burhan illustrates generality with two idha examples."}, {"id": "6:68/q03/p3", "position": "Emphatic nun is strictly required after this conditional.", "reasons": "Samin attributes this to al-Zajjaj and rejects it on poetic and grammatical grounds; no one requires specifically the heavy form."}, {"id": "6:68/q03/p4", "position": "Idha itself makes the ban recur whenever mockery resumes.", "reasons": "Some scholars infer this; Alusi says recurrence instead follows from tying the rule to its occasion."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q04", "question": "Why is 'when' used first and 'if' for forgetting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q04/p1", "position": "Mockery is expected, whereas forgetting is merely possible.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi contrast idha with in; Samin adds prophetic protection. Bursevi says the wording does not establish an actual lapse. Biqaʿi and Ibn Ashur see emphasis on the order."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q05", "question": "Who are those engaging in the signs?", "turns_on": "Whether the historical mockers were polytheists, People of the Book, or sectarian disputants, and whether the description extends by conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q05/p1", "position": "They are Meccan polytheists, especially Quraysh.", "reasons": "Tabari, Suddi, Kashshaf, Nasafi, Alusi and Elmalili identify them; Ibn Ashur limits withdrawal to fierce public attackers, since shunning every denier would halt preaching."}, {"id": "6:68/q05/p2", "position": "They are sectarian innovators or people of disputation.", "reasons": "Muhammad or Ibn Sirin associates revelation with people of passions; Abu Jaʿfar and Muhammad ibn ʿAli apply it to disputants. Tabatabaʾi says reports generalize the underlying cause."}, {"id": "6:68/q05/p3", "position": "They are People of the Book or Jews speaking falsely about the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Mujahid and later transmitters specify People of the Book; Ibn Jawzi specifies Jews. Alusi says their habit resembles the polytheists'."}, {"id": "6:68/q05/p4", "position": "The description applies to anyone who mocks signs, whatever their affiliation.", "reasons": "Ibn Khuwayz Mindad includes believer and unbeliever; Tabatabaʾi extends the rule by rationale. Some reports link it with believers' divisive debate in 6:65."}, {"id": "6:68/q05/p5", "position": "In an inward reading, they project the self's knowledge and power onto divine signs.", "reasons": "Qashani calls them veiled associators, whose companionship risks veiling."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q06", "question": "What are the signs at issue?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q06/p1", "position": "They are the Qur'an and its revelations.", "reasons": "Muqatil ibn Hayyan, Ibn Jawzi and Bursevi state this; Tabari adds insulting the Messenger."}, {"id": "6:68/q06/p2", "position": "They are God's religion or signs more generally.", "reasons": "Hasan and Saʿid describe denial of God's signs and religion; Tabatabaʾi speaks of God's true signs."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q07", "question": "What does khawd mean in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether it is disparaging talk, denial, or theological debate.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q07/p1", "position": "It is mocking, denying, insulting, or falsely disputing revelation.", "reasons": "Mujahid stresses mockery, Suddi denial, Tabari both. Raghib, Islahi and Study Quran cite Quranic parallels including 9:65, 4:140 and 6:91."}, {"id": "6:68/q07/p2", "position": "It includes contentious religious debate.", "reasons": "Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn Abbas warn against disputants and division; a Tabatabaʾi report adds storytellers. {"id": "6:68/q09", "question": "Why is a relative clause used for the mockers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q09/p1", "position": "Their defining conduct supplies the reason and endpoint for withdrawal.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says it singles out the abusive subset after 6:66 and ends the ban when they cease. {"id": "6:68/q10", "question": "What event prompted the withdrawal order?", "turns_on": "Reports differ in who was present and how the mockery arose.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q10/p1", "position": "Polytheists insulted or mocked the Prophet and Qur'an while sitting with believers.", "reasons": "Suddi, Ibn Abbas, Saʿid and Muqatil transmit this; Muqatil says believers feared staying implied assent. Nahhas and Qurtubi say the Prophet had sat to admonish them."}, {"id": "6:68/q10/p2", "position": "Muslims feared leaving would prevent sitting or circumambulating in the Sacred Mosque.", "reasons": "Abu Jaʿfar says 6:69 then permitted reminding and teaching as possible; Baydawi, Kashshaf and Bursevi report this concern."}, {"id": "6:68/q10/p3", "position": "Polytheists came to hear the Prophet, then mocked.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj says revelation followed; another report says his rising frightened them into warning one another to stop."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q11", "question": "What action does 'turn away' require?", "turns_on": "Whether withdrawal must be physical departure or may be another clear display of disapproval.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q11/p1", "position": "Leave the gathering and do not remain seated or listen.", "reasons": "Jishumi glosses iʿrad as turning away, near sadd and opposite iqbal. {"id": "6:68/q12", "question": "When may one sit with them again?", "turns_on": "Whether any change of topic suffices or permissible non-mocking talk is required.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q12/p1", "position": "When discussion changes away from mockery or signs, the temporary ban ends.", "reasons": "Muqatil says other than God's matter and remembrance; Kashshaf explicitly permits sitting again; Nasafi specifies permissible talk. {"id": "6:68/q13", "question": "What does the pronoun in 'other than it' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether its antecedent is the signs as discourse, or the understood act of khawd or mockery.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q13/p1", "position": "It returns to the signs understood as Qur'an, speech or discourse.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Abu al-Baqa, Bursevi and Alusi explain why masculine singular can stand for plural signs."}, {"id": "6:68/q13/p2", "position": "It returns to khawd, the act of engaging in talk.", "reasons": "Samin derives the noun from the preceding verb and cites a parallel where safah is understood from foolish; Alusi prefers this antecedent, and Tabatabaʾi calls it the prohibited discourse."}, {"id": "6:68/q13/p3", "position": "It returns specifically to mockery.", "reasons": "Al-Hawfi cites a poem about a fool running toward folly when warned away."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q14", "question": "Why withdraw from the mockery?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q14/p1", "position": "Withdrawal publicly repudiates abuse and avoids fruitless argument or complicity.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says argument in that state misplaces proof; Qurtubi says leave when advice cannot be accepted. Islahi says debate fuels frenzy, silence dishonors truth and risks hypocrisy; Tabatabaʾi cites 4:140, where sitting makes one like them."}, {"id": "6:68/q14/p2", "position": "Withdrawal protects inward communion from veiling.", "reasons": "Qashani warns that company may cause a shift into their veil; Qushayri urges the realized to keep intimate communion with God."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q15", "question": "How broadly does the rule apply to other harmful gatherings?", "turns_on": "Whether the ban extends beyond mockers to sinners, innovators or other harmful speech.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q15/p1", "position": "It extends by its rationale to innovators, open wrongdoers and hostile speech.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi reject associating with sinners while endorsing their views as dissimulation. Al-Fudayl warns against loving, marrying into, or sitting with innovators; ʿAisha's reported hadith condemns honoring one. Study Quran points to false adultery gossip in 24:14–16 as a cause of injustice, division and mistrust."}, {"id": "6:68/q15/p2", "position": "The ban lasts for the time and conduct of mockery, allowing a sound purpose otherwise.", "reasons": "Tabatabaʾi says it is not a permanent ban on every gathering; Kuranyolu permits ordinary association when values are not insulted."}, {"id": "6:68/q15/p3", "position": "In severe fear, a person other than the Messenger may be excused; the Messenger must leave.", "reasons": "Razi argues excusing the Messenger would undermine trust in obligations he conveyed, while another person's lapse would not."}, {"id": "6:68/q15/p4", "position": "One should leave despite fear of ridicule for abandoning debate.", "reasons": "Islahi likens tolerating abuse of God to tolerating abuse of parents; prolonged debate can serve ego."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q16", "question": "How does the command relate to 4:140 and surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "Whether 4:140 repeats, explains, changes or supersedes the rule.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q16/p1", "position": "Verse 4:140 repeats or clarifies the rule against sitting with mockers.", "reasons": "Tabari links 4:140 and 4:63; Ibn Kathir and Tabatabaʾi say shared sitting resembles approval. Study Quran notes possible links to factions in 6:65."}, {"id": "6:68/q16/p4", "position": "Verse 4:140 abrogated this early command; a fighting command followed.", "reasons": "Balkhi prefers abrogation when Muslims were few; Suddi adds 9:5 after 4:140."}, {"id": "6:68/q16/p5", "position": "The Prophet's role remains warning through revelation rather than forcing belief.", "reasons": "Islahi says he should disregard new demands and preach at a receptive time."}]}

{"id": "6:68/q19", "question": "What does Satan make one forget?", "turns_on": "Whether the forgotten thing is the revealed prohibition or alleged rational aversion before revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q19/p1", "position": "The prohibition on sitting with mockers or withdrawing.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Tabrisi, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi say Satan distracts from the command, so one remains seated. {"id": "6:68/q20", "question": "Who is Satan here, and how can forgetting be ascribed to him?", "turns_on": "Whether Satan causes a human lapse indirectly or cannot influence the Prophet at all.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q20/p1", "position": "Satan can indirectly cause natural forgetfulness without controlling revelation or causing sin.", "reasons": "Tabrisi attributes forgetfulness to God but says neglected thought and whispers provide an occasion, like death from exposing someone to cold. {"id": "6:68/q21", "question": "Can the Prophet forget, and in what matters?", "turns_on": "Whether lapse is possible in ordinary actions, worship or law, and whether conveying revelation is protected.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q21/p1", "position": "He can forget in action, worship or legal practice, but God corrects him.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports Adam's forgetting, the Prophet's saying he forgets as a human, and recitation that reminded him of a verse. Bursevi claims scholarly agreement."}, {"id": "6:68/q21/p2", "position": "He cannot forget in conveying revelation, but may lapse elsewhere if religion remains intact.", "reasons": "Tabrisi states the Imami rule, comparing sleep and fainting. {"id": "6:68/q22", "question": "When must God correct a prophetic lapse?", "turns_on": "Whether correction must be immediate or may occur later in his lifetime.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q22/p1", "position": "Correction must accompany the event immediately.", "reasons": "Qadi Abu Bakr and most scholars require it; Alusi reports the same majority, and Nawawi favors prompt correction to prevent harm."}, {"id": "6:68/q22/p2", "position": "Correction may be delayed, but before his life and transmission end.", "reasons": "Abu al-Maʿali and another group permit this interval."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q23", "question": "Can prophets err in ordinary speech or worldly beliefs?", "turns_on": "Whether protection from error extends beyond revelation to all reports and ordinary beliefs.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q23/p1", "position": "A prophet may forget ordinary speech unrelated to revelation, law or eschatological report.", "reasons": "Alusi reports a group arguing no religious harm results."}, {"id": "6:68/q23/p2", "position": "Prophets cannot err in any report, in any state.", "reasons": "Qadi Iyad argues their speech was preserved, and no verbal correction is transmitted, unlike corrections in prayer, date-palm advice and Badr's position."}, {"id": "6:68/q23/p3", "position": "Inadvertence in worldly beliefs is possible.", "reasons": "Qadi Iyad does not rule it out."}]}

{"id": "6:68/q26", "question": "How is dhikra parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether it is accusative or nominative, and how its form is classified.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q26/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun on the rare fuʿlā pattern.", "reasons": "Samin says it is the only such verbal noun; Bursevi repeats this."}, {"id": "6:68/q26/p2", "position": "It may be accusative by an implied command to remind, or nominative in 'a reminder is upon you'.", "reasons": "Tabrisi cites 42:48 for the predicative possibility."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q27", "question": "What does 'after the reminder' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether it means recollecting the ban, God's reminding of rational ugliness, or admonishing offenders.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q27/p1", "position": "After remembering God's prohibition and duty to withdraw.", "reasons": "Abu Malik and Jubbaʾi state this; Baydawi, Alusi's majority and Ibn Ashur concur."}, {"id": "6:68/q27/p2", "position": "After God reminds one that sitting with mockers is ugly.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari ties this to pre-revelation rational prohibition; Alusi calls it remote."}, {"id": "6:68/q27/p3", "position": "After reminding them by inviting them to faith.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim says withdraw when further appeal is hopeless; Alusi rejects it."}]}
